text: On December fifth, nineteen fifty-two, a fog rolled in — and it never left.
London heated itself with coal, and that winter, it burned more than ever.
A wall of warm air pressed down from above, trapping the smoke at street level.
Every day, a thousand tonnes of smoke and acid filled the air.
The fog turned yellow, thick as pea soup.
People could not see their own feet.
Buses stopped. Conductors walked ahead with torches, guiding drivers through the dark.
The smog seeped indoors. Theatres cancelled their shows. Cinemas went dark.
At the Smithfield Show, prize cattle gasped for breath where they stood.
Hospitals filled with people who could not breathe.
On December ninth, the wind returned, and the fog lifted.
The government counted four thousand dead. The true number was closer to twelve thousand.
London came back. But twelve thousand people never did.
Four years later, Britain passed the Clean Air Act — the first law of its kind in the world.
Would you have gone outside in that fog?
